passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it allows courts to enforce promises that would otherwise be unenforceable for want of consideration. The classical theory of contract, rooted in the exchange model inherited from nineteenth-century English jurisprudence, holds that a promise is legally binding only when it is supported by consideration — that is, when the promisee gives something of value in return for the promisor's commitment. Promissory estoppel disrupts this scheme by protecting a promisee who, receiving no formal exchange, nonetheless relies on a promise to his or her substantial detriment. The doctrine therefore raises a persistent theoretical question: whether the enforcement of such promises reflects a genuine departure from the consideration requirement or merely a subsidiary equitable remedy that leaves the classical model largely intact.

American courts in the twentieth century generally treated promissory estoppel as a narrow exception, confined to cases in which the reliance was both foreseeable and substantial. The Restatement (Second) of Contracts, published by the American Law Institute in 1981, codified this approach in Section 90, which conditions enforcement on a showing that the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee's reliance, that the reliance in fact occurred, and that injustice can be avoided only by enforcement. Courts applying Section 90 have, however, reached strikingly inconsistent results. In some jurisdictions, the remedy awarded is full expectation damages — placing the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed. In others, courts limit recovery to reliance damages — reimbursing only the out-of-pocket losses attributable to the promisee's detrimental reliance. This divergence is not merely technical; it reflects a deeper disagreement about whether promissory estoppel is a substitute for contract or a tort-like remedy for harm caused by broken undertakings.

The inconsistency in remedial outcomes is, regrettably, traceable in part to the ambiguity of Section 90 itself, which states only that the remedy granted "may be limited as justice requires" without specifying the circumstances that warrant limitation. Some commentators have argued that this language was deliberately flexible, designed to allow courts to calibrate relief to the equities of each case. But this defense of open-ended discretion comes at the cost of predictability, and predictability is a value that commercial actors, who must assess the enforceability of their undertakings in advance, depend on heavily. One hopes that appellate courts will eventually provide clearer guidance on the conditions under which expectation damages, rather than the more limited reliance measure, are appropriate — not merely as a matter of doctrinal tidiness, but because the practical stakes for those who reorganize their affairs in reliance on another's assurance are often considerable.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts, Section 90, introduced promissory estoppel into American contract law by replacing the consideration requirement with a reliance-based standard.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Promissory estoppel has generated inconsistent judicial outcomes because courts disagree about whether it is a true contract substitute or a tort-like remedy, a problem worsened by the ambiguity of its codified formulation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Appellate courts should adopt a uniform rule awarding expectation damages in all promissory estoppel cases to promote predictability in commercial transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The classical consideration requirement in contract law has been effectively abolished in American jurisdictions that follow the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as a narrow equitable exception that preserves the integrity of the classical exchange model in all but the most extreme cases of detrimental reliance.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the theoretical tension over promissory estoppel's status (contract substitute vs. tort remedy), documents the inconsistent remedial outcomes this produces, and locates the root cause in Section 90's ambiguity — all of which B captures across the full passage.
explanations.A: Too narrow and inaccurate: the passage does not say Section 90 introduced promissory estoppel or that it 'replaced' the consideration requirement; it describes Section 90 as a codification of an approach already in use.
explanations.C: This states only the author's closing suggestion, which is a recommendation appearing at the end — not the main point integrating all three paragraphs.
explanations.D: Overstates: the passage says the consideration requirement is disrupted or complicated, not abolished.
explanations.E: This describes one view mentioned in the passage (the 'narrow exception' view of American courts) but not the passage's overall argument, which challenges the adequacy of that view.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the open-ended discretion afforded to courts by Section 90's remedial language can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic approval, because flexibility allows courts to respond equitably to the unique facts of each case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism, because while the flexibility may serve equitable goals, it undermines the predictability that commercial actors require.

choices.label: C
choices.text: strong condemnation, because deliberate ambiguity in statutory language is an abdication of legislative responsibility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cautious approval, because predictability is less important in contract law than fairness to individual parties.

choices.label: E
choices.text: studied neutrality, because the author presents both the advantages and disadvantages of open-ended discretion without endorsing either view.

explanations.correct: The author acknowledges the commentators' defense of flexibility ('deliberately flexible, designed to allow courts to calibrate relief') but immediately counters that 'this defense of open-ended discretion comes at the cost of predictability' — signaling qualified skepticism rather than outright condemnation or approval.
explanations.A: Overstates positivity: the author acknowledges but does not endorse the flexibility argument.
explanations.C: Too strong: 'regrettably' signals concern, but the author never accuses the drafters of abdication or condemns the ambiguity in such harsh terms.
explanations.D: Inverts the author's position: the author treats predictability as a weighty value, not a lesser one.
explanations.E: Wrong valence: the author does take a side — the final sentence ('one hopes') and the criticism of unpredictability reveal a clear, if measured, evaluative stance.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its theoretical tension identified; the doctrine's codification and resulting judicial inconsistency are described; the source of that inconsistency is diagnosed and a remedy suggested.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical overview of contract law is provided; two competing schools of judicial thought are described and evaluated; the author endorses one school over the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrinal exception is criticized; a legislative solution is proposed; possible objections to that solution are considered and rejected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A classical legal model is explained; a court case is used to illustrate its application; the author proposes a reform of the classical model.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two opposing definitions of promissory estoppel are stated; their practical consequences are compared; the author concludes that both definitions are inadequate.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its theoretical tension (contract substitute vs. equitable exception); paragraph 2 describes Section 90's codification and the inconsistent remedial outcomes it has produced; paragraph 3 diagnoses the ambiguity in Section 90 as the cause and closes with the author's suggestion for clearer appellate guidance.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing and inaccuracy: the passage does not provide a general historical overview as its opening move, nor does it endorse one school of judicial thought over another as a final move.
explanations.C: Wrong: the passage does not propose a legislative solution, nor does it consider and reject objections to such a proposal.
explanations.D: Wrong grain: the passage's main analytical work is about the doctrine's inconsistent application, not about illustrating the classical model with a specific court case.
explanations.E: Wrong: the passage does not conclude that both definitions of promissory estoppel are inadequate; its concern is with remedial inconsistency and doctrinal ambiguity, not the definitions themselves.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition imposed by Section 90 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts for enforcement of a promise under promissory estoppel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee must demonstrate that she offered something of value in exchange for the promisor's commitment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisor must have had actual knowledge that the promisee would rely on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisor should reasonably have expected that the promisee would rely on the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The remedy awarded must be limited to the promisee's out-of-pocket losses rather than full expectation damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promise must have been made in a commercial context in which predictability of enforcement is especially important.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Section 90 conditions enforcement on 'a showing that the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee's reliance' — a reasonable foreseeability standard, not an actual-knowledge standard.
explanations.A: This describes the classical consideration requirement, which Section 90 displaces — the opposite of what the question asks.
explanations.B: Alters a qualifier: the passage says 'reasonably have expected' (an objective standard), not 'actual knowledge' (a subjective one) — a classic altered-qualifier trap.
explanations.D: Confuses the remedial question (which the passage says is left open by 'as justice requires') with an affirmative condition for enforcement.
explanations.E: A plausible world claim the passage never makes; Section 90's conditions do not include a commercial-context requirement.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a court awarding full expectation damages in a promissory estoppel case would most likely be committed to which of the following views?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be treated as functionally equivalent to a fully enforceable contract rather than as a tort-like remedy for detrimental reliance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The classical consideration requirement is an outdated formalism that should be abandoned entirely in favor of a reliance-based theory of contract obligation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Predictability in commercial transactions is the paramount value in contract law and must override equitable concerns in every case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Section 90 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts was poorly drafted and should be replaced with a more precise statutory formulation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliance damages are in all cases a more appropriate remedy than expectation damages because they avoid conferring a windfall on the promisee.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the divergence between expectation and reliance damages 'reflects a deeper disagreement about whether promissory estoppel is a substitute for contract or a tort-like remedy.' Awarding full expectation damages — placing the promisee where she would have been had the promise been performed — logically reflects the view that the doctrine operates as a contract substitute.
explanations.B: Overreaches: endorsing expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases does not commit a court to abandoning the consideration requirement altogether; the two questions are distinct.
explanations.C: Inverts: the passage associates the predictability concern with the author's critique of Section 90's ambiguity, not with the choice of expectation over reliance damages.
explanations.D: Outside scope: a court's remedial choice does not necessarily imply a view about Section 90's drafting quality.
explanations.E: Reverses: this describes the rationale for reliance damages, not expectation damages — the opposite of what the question asks.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'commercial actors, who must assess the enforceability of their undertakings in advance' (third paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kind of sophisticated party for whom promissory estoppel was originally designed as a protective doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a concrete class of actors whose interests are specifically harmed by the doctrinal inconsistency the author has described, thereby reinforcing the practical stakes of that inconsistency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that commercial parties are better equipped than individual promisees to absorb the costs of broken promises without judicial relief.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast commercial actors with non-commercial parties to suggest that promissory estoppel should apply differently depending on the context.

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the argument that predictability is a value unique to commercial law and therefore irrelevant to the equitable concerns that Section 90 was designed to address.

explanations.correct: Immediately before this reference, the author argues that open-ended discretion 'comes at the cost of predictability.' The reference to commercial actors who need to assess enforceability in advance concretizes and reinforces this cost, showing who specifically is harmed by unpredictability — thus amplifying the critique of Section 90's ambiguity.
explanations.A: Accurate content, wrong function: the passage does not describe commercial actors as promissory estoppel's target beneficiaries; rather, they exemplify why predictability matters.
explanations.C: Reverses the point: the author treats commercial actors as a reason to demand more predictability, not as parties capable of absorbing broken promises.
explanations.D: The passage draws no contrast between commercial and non-commercial parties regarding differential application of the doctrine.
explanations.E: Inverts the function: the author uses commercial actors to show predictability is important broadly, not to suggest it is irrelevant to equitable concerns.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the ambiguity of Section 90's remedial language is a significant source of the inconsistency in promissory estoppel outcomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several jurisdictions that apply Section 90 have adopted supplementary common-law rules that specify when expectation damages rather than reliance damages are appropriate, yet those jurisdictions continue to produce divergent outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal scholars who participated in drafting Section 90 have stated in published writings that the 'as justice requires' language was intended to provide flexibility rather than to impose any particular remedial measure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in jurisdictions that have replaced Section 90 with more precisely worded statutes have shown no greater consistency in remedial outcomes than courts applying Section 90.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The divergence between expectation and reliance damages in promissory estoppel cases was well documented in case law published before the American Law Institute began drafting the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel cases constitute only a small fraction of all contract disputes litigated in American courts each year.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that Section 90's ambiguous remedial language is a significant cause of inconsistency. If courts operating under more precisely worded statutes show no greater consistency, that suggests the ambiguity of Section 90's language is not the operative cause of divergent outcomes — the inconsistency arises from something else, undermining the author's causal diagnosis.
explanations.A: This might seem to weaken the claim, but if supplementary rules exist yet inconsistency persists, that actually reinforces the idea that clarity is hard to achieve — it does not specifically exonerate Section 90's language as the source of the problem.
explanations.B: This supports rather than undermines the author's characterization of Section 90's language as deliberately flexible; it does not challenge the claim that this flexibility causes inconsistency.
explanations.D: This shows the inconsistency predates Section 90, which might suggest the doctrine itself (not the codification's language) is the source of divergence — a partial weakener. However, it does not as directly target the causal role of Section 90's specific remedial language as C does.
explanations.E: Irrelevant to the author's causal claim; the frequency of such cases does not bear on whether Section 90's ambiguity causes inconsistency when those cases do arise.
